Q10.prompt: For a small FPGA project I want to detect rising edges from a button input. My prereq evidence is that I drew a two-flop synchronizer with help, and I have no board yet. What is one next milestone and how will I know I reached it?
criteria: Names a concrete simulated/traceable milestone and an observable pass/fail test for a rising edge, rather than claiming hardware success.
Matches the reported help level; treats debouncing or synchronization limits accurately if raised and does not claim independent readiness.

responses.A:
One next milestone: build and simulate a two-flop synchronizer followed by a rising-edge detector. The target is one clock-cycle pulse for each low-to-high transition of the synchronized signal.

Before testing, set these acceptance criteria: no pulse after reset while the input stays low; one pulse when the synchronized signal rises; no repeated pulses while it stays high; no pulse when it falls; and a second pulse after another rise. Compare the waveform against those expected events, including a button transition between clock edges.

Your helped diagram is evidence of assisted setup. A passing simulation would establish digital behavior under the tested conditions; hardware timing, metastability reliability, and switch bounce remain untested without further checks. This milestone detects edges, so a bouncing button may produce multiple pulses.
responses.B:
One next milestone: simulate a synchronous rising-edge detector fed by your two-flop synchronizer. Define its output to pulse for one clock cycle when the synchronized signal changes from 0 to 1. Assume reset initializes all stored values to 0, and defer button debouncing to a separate milestone.

Before running the simulation, draw the expected output for a synchronized input that stays low, rises and stays high, falls, then rises again. The acceptance criteria follow from that specification: no pulse while low, exactly one one-cycle pulse per rise, no repeated pulses while held high, and no pulse on a fall. Include reset while the input is low to expose an initialization error.

Compare the predicted and simulated traces, and explain how the stored previous sample detects a rise. Your synchronizer drawing was assisted; this checkpoint can establish simulation behavior and show your own reasoning separately. Without a board, physical button behavior, bounce, and hardware operation remain untested.
responses.C:
One next milestone: simulate a synchronized rising-edge detector and explain its trace. Your assisted synchronizer drawing is useful preparation; independent design and hardware behavior remain untested.

Assume a single clock, active-high synchronous reset, and a button signal that stays high for several clock cycles. Use two synchronizer stages, then compare the synchronized signal with its previous sampled value.

Before simulation, predict the trace. From the requirement “one pulse per sampled low-to-high transition,” acceptance means: no pulse during reset or while low; one clock-cycle pulse after a rising transition propagates through the synchronizer; no repeated pulses while held high; no pulse on release; and a new pulse on a second press. Compare those predictions with the waveform, including a check that holding the button high does not hold the pulse high.

Reaching this milestone supports the simulated digital behavior and whatever reasoning you demonstrate. It does not verify physical metastability performance or button debouncing; a bouncing button can still produce multiple detected edges.
responses.D:
One next milestone: simulate a rising-edge detector after a two-flop synchronizer, under an explicit assumption that the button signal is already debounced. Synchronization alone does not remove button bounce.

Before running it, write the expected trace: after the synchronized signal changes from 0 to 1, the detector produces exactly one clock-cycle pulse; holding it high produces no further pulses, a falling edge produces none, and a second rise produces one new pulse. Define reset to clear both synchronizer stages and the detector history, and include reset in the test.

You reach the implementation milestone when the simulated trace matches those expectations. Explain why the detector compares the current synchronized value with its previous value. Record any help used: your earlier drawing was assisted, and a passing simulation would not establish unaided design skill or physical button reliability. Hardware behavior and metastability performance remain untested without a board.
responses.E:
One next milestone: implement and simulate a two-flop synchronizer followed by a rising-edge detector, with a defined reset state. Your assisted drawing supports starting this task; it doesn't yet establish independent implementation.

Define success before testing: after reset, the output stays low for a held-low input; each low-to-high transition of the synchronized signal produces exactly one clock-cycle pulse; holding it high produces no further pulses; falling edges produce none. Exercise changes between clock edges and inspect waveforms against those requirements.

This establishes simulated behavior. RTL simulation doesn't establish metastability reliability, and a physical button can bounce: one pulse per press needs a separate debounce requirement. Board behavior remains untested.
responses.F:
One next milestone: implement and simulate a synchronized button rising-edge detector that produces one clock-cycle pulse for each sampled low-to-high transition. Your assisted synchronizer drawing is a starting point; independent implementation is still untested.

Before running the simulation, predict a clock-by-clock trace using this specification: two synchronizer stages, one register storing the previous synchronized value, pulse = synchronized value AND NOT previous value, and synchronous reset clearing all three registers.

You'll have reached the simulation milestone when the trace matches those predictions: reset gives no pulse, a held high input gives exactly one pulse, a falling edge gives none, and a later rise gives another. Check the pulse occurs at the synchronizer's expected latency and lasts one clock period.

A passing simulation supports the logic under that model. It doesn't test physical metastability or button bounce; a bouncing button may produce multiple pulses. Board checks remain open.
